It's that nothing arrives clearly enough now to trust — you can't sort what's genuinely offered from what's expected, so the safest move has been to send nothing out.

What sharpens is attention, not generosity. One thing at a time, until the fog has edges. Solitude helps here; alone, you can tell what's yours and what's theirs without anyone watching. Then the exchange can start again, small. Notice one thing that's genuinely offered to you, and let it land before you think about what you owe back.
3.sheetLine: You stopped giving when you stopped being able to tell what was fair.

4.tense: You are already trading fairly with people around you, and you talk about it like it's just how things work.
4.verb: Passing what is given back and forth until it comes out even
4.place: In the fog where the next step is visible and the far end is not
4.ask: Tell one person a plain thing you feel about the two of you — no preamble, no question attached — and let it sit.
4.core:
You're already keeping it even. You adjust, you give, you take — and if someone asked, you'd say that's just being decent. But the fairness you're running is yours. You decided, somewhere, what counts and how much, and you've been calling it common sense.

A hunch about what's fair shows up before you can argue for it, and it's right often enough that you act on it without checking twice. What's off now is that you do it silently. You feel the balance between you and someone and say nothing, so the judgment stays invisible, even to you. Say one of those things plainly, without dressing it as a question. What you felt holds up. It just hasn't been claimed.
4.sheetLine: You're already keeping it even. You call it common sense.

1.tense: You are keeping the exchange honest right now, in both directions.
1.verb: give and receive so the exchange stays honest
1.place: where you're becoming what you actually are
1.ask: Name one thing you gave this week and one thing you let yourself receive, out loud, to the person it came from.
1.core:
You know how to make an exchange without measuring it. Something gets offered, you feel what's fair, and you answer from that rather than from a scorecard — giving when it's yours to give, taking when it's yours to take. In the part of life where you're becoming what you are, that steadiness is the ground under your feet.

The books stay honest and people stay in reach. You give without going under and receive without flinching, and afterwards nobody has to go back and fix it. You also stop checking whether the fairness reads as fairness and just fine-tune as you go.

What keeps this alive is you showing your hand now and then. Say where a thing came from. Say thanks once, plainly, instead of letting a kindness pass like a bus.
1.sheetLine: You keep the exchange fair by feeling it, not by counting.

2.tense: You are running the accounts of every exchange before the exchange has happened.
2.verb: give and receive so the exchange stays honest
2.place: where you're becoming what you actually are
2.ask: Pick one open exchange and leave it alone for a day — no adjusting, no evening-out — and see what it looks like on its own.
2.core:
You can see what's fair here, and you're using that to get ahead of everything. You know what you're owed, what you've given, what the other person will probably do — so you start evening things out before they've had their turn. The fairness is real. The calculation has gotten loud.

Fairness works by handshake when it's left alone: you do your part, they do theirs, and you don't replay it at midnight. What's happening instead is you bracing against a version of the exchange that hasn't arrived, correcting for it, holding the balance up by yourself.

Setting it down for a day is not giving up your sense of what's fair. It's finding out which parts of this exchange you're actually carrying, and which parts are just the future you've written ahead of time.
2.sheetLine: You're evening out an exchange that hasn't happened yet.

3.tense: Something stopped reaching across to other people a while back, and it hasn't started again.
3.verb: give and receive so the exchange stays honest
3.place: where you're becoming what you actually are
3.ask: Sign up for one recurring thing — a class, a league, a standing call — and keep the first three sessions on the calendar.
3.core:
There's a fairness in you that used to move between you and other people, and right now it stays inside. You can see what's fair. You can see what you'd give. It doesn't come out, and nothing comes back in, and the part of you that's becoming what you are has gone quiet in that direction.

Giving and receiving move at the same pace when the line is open — you reach out, someone reaches back, and neither of you has to think about it. What's here instead is a road with traffic going one way, or two people not reaching at all.

Pushing yourself to give more isn't the move. Pick something that happens on a schedule, show up whether or not you feel like it, and let the contact do what deciding can't.
3.sheetLine: The fairness is still in you. It's just stopped traveling.

4.tense: You are already keeping the exchange fair between people and calling it something else.
4.verb: give and receive so the exchange stays honest
4.place: where you're becoming what you actually are
4.ask: Catch one thing you did today because it was fair and say it plainly, as yours — 'I did that because it was right' — to whoever's nearby.
4.core:
You keep things even without noticing you're doing it. You feel when someone's had more than their share, you adjust, you give back in a way that doesn't feel like generosity because it feels like the obvious thing. People around you lean on that more than they say.

When it runs clean, it isn't a principle you're applying — it's a direct sense of what's owed, and it lands without argument. What's happening instead is you calling it 'just how it works,' or 'the way we do things,' as if it were the room's habit rather than something you're doing.

That's not modesty. It's a choice you're making and leaving unsigned, which means you don't get to know your own hand in it — or let anyone else in on it.
4.sheetLine: You keep things fair and file it under how things work.

1.tense: You are standing at fair exchange and can see the whole shape of it.
1.verb: trading fairly through the felt exchange between people
1.place: from the moment the whole shape arrives before anyone has named it
1.ask: Name one exchange you and another have already settled, in one sentence, out loud, before the day gets loud.
1.core:
You are standing in a fair exchange where giving and receiving have come back level, and you can see the whole shape of the trade while you stand inside it. The line where one side stopped and the other began is visible to you without any effort. That cuts both ways. You can call a bad trade early, and you can leave a good one alone instead of evening it out one more time.

When the pattern is held loosely, the exchange itself is trusted. One side gives today, the other gives tomorrow, and you let that be true. The measure stays loose and the trade still works. Feed that. The task is not to hold the line tighter; it is to let one exchange stand at what it already is when it comes up next, and not one adjustment past that.
1.sheetLine: You can see the fair exchange and you are standing in it.

2.tense: You are ahead of the fairness, deciding what each side will owe before anything has actually moved.
2.verb: trading fairly through the felt exchange between people
2.place: from the moment the whole shape arrives before anyone has named it
2.ask: Leave one exchange you have already weighed exactly where it stands, and do not add a single item to either side before it moves again.
2.core:
You are running the math ahead of the exchange. The balance is not here yet, but you have already worked out what each side owes and what you will have to do to make it fair. So a conversation can turn into an audit, and a kindness comes pre-paid with a number on it. You are carrying the whole ledger instead of letting it pass between you.

Somewhere ahead there is a settling up that would let you rest. That settling keeps moving because the math is going on in your head, not between two people. The fair thing is usually a clear read on what is right, and it changes with the exchange in front of you. Hold one trade this week without improving it.
2.sheetLine: You are balancing a trade that has not happened yet.

3.tense: You have been silent at a door where giving and receiving once moved between you.
3.verb: trading fairly through the felt exchange between people
3.place: from the moment the whole shape arrives before anyone has named it
3.ask: Pick one small exchange with someone you trust and take only your side of it, once, without working out what will come back.
3.core:
You have been quiet at the place where trades happen. Giving and receiving have felt like something to keep track of, so you stopped putting much into the circle. Now you mostly give or mostly hold back, and the exchange does not really start. What is missing is not generosity; it is the ability to be part of a fair trade, even badly.

When the exchange is working, one motion carries both sides, and you can enter it without deciding the outcome first. Pick one small thing and take only your side of it. Say what you sent, without asking about the return, and let it have its own life from there.
3.sheetLine: You are not entering the exchange and calling it fine.

4.tense: You are already reading the pattern through what is given and what is returned.
4.verb: trading fairly through the felt exchange between people
4.place: from the moment the whole shape arrives before anyone has named it
4.ask: Say out loud the one trade where your own reading was right, before you go back to keeping it to yourself.
4.core:
You are already reading the shape of what is fair between people. You catch the small signal — a word, a moment, something two people will not say — and you know what it means about who is giving and who is taking before it is spoken. You keep it to yourself and call it just how things are, but the reading is there and it is yours.

The pattern you see is what fairness looks like from where you sit. The exchange runs on what you know, without anyone saying what they know, so the trade goes on with no one owning the truth that moved in it. The confirmation lands without argument when it is said, and saying it out loud makes it truer, not harder. Name one trade and your read of it.
4.sheetLine: You see what is fair and you have not said how you know.

1.tense: You are handing over something finished, and you know what it cost to make.
1.verb: offering what you made for what you need, and taking what is offered
1.place: the moment a finished thing leaves your hands
1.ask: Offer one thing you made — a meal, a plan, a repair — and when someone moves to give back, let them. Don't wave it off, don't match it in the same breath. Take the return and let the thing be even.
1.core:
You're at the end of making something, and it finishes where it meets another person. Not the second you stop working — the second it lands with someone and they take it in. You know what went into it, and you're still in the room while they weigh it.

What gets in the way is the extra step. You hand something over, then hand over more to make the first one comfortable — topping it up, sending back whatever comes, keeping one hand on it after it leaves. Open hands that are also braced. The staying power you need now sits in the receiving. Letting something be paid for is its own kind of strength.
1.sheetLine: You made it, you handed it over, and you're letting them take it in.

2.tense: You're already paying for things tomorrow, and no one has held out a hand yet.
2.verb: offering what you made for what you need, and taking what is offered
2.place: the moment a finished thing leaves your hands
2.ask: Pick one thing you were about to give, and don't give it yet. Wait until someone actually asks or offers. Let the day pass with it ungiven.
2.core:
A hand goes out and a hand comes back at about the same pace. You offer, they take, something returns, and neither person holds the whole thing up alone. There's a bottom to what you put in and a bottom to what comes back.

What's happening instead is that you've moved the exchange ahead of the clock. Someone might need something, so you've already decided what you'll hand over, already felt the cost, already written how they'll answer. You're holding out things nobody reached for. There's an edge of bracing to it — not free, but fortified against a future where you come up short. What's needed here is strength that holds still rather than reaches. A shoulder that bears weight without grabbing the load. Let the other hand open first.
2.sheetLine: You're settling accounts that haven't been opened.

3.tense: You stopped putting things into the shared stream a while back, and you can still see the spot.
3.verb: offering what you made for what you need, and taking what is offered
3.place: the moment a finished thing leaves your hands
3.ask: Take one small skill you have — measuring, listening, fixing — and use it on something that isn't yours. Your neighbor's gate, a friend's essay, the office plant.
3.core:
You're holding what you made close, and not much is moving between you and anyone. You know the give-and-take is supposed to work, but you're standing off the road watching traffic go by without you in it. This is where something gets finished and let out into the open — yours is closing inward.

The muscle that's gone is attention. You can still notice what's fair and what isn't, you're just not aiming that noticing at anything shared. Practice that stays home sharpens you and walls you in at the same time. Point the eye at something outside your own head and handing things over starts to feel less like risk and more like ordinary traffic.
3.sheetLine: You've gone quiet at the exact point where things are supposed to move.

4.tense: You're already keeping the exchange even on both sides, and you file it under being reasonable.
4.verb: offering what you made for what you need, and taking what is offered
4.place: the moment a finished thing leaves your hands
4.ask: Catch yourself doing one thing that keeps an exchange even — waiting your turn, paying back, splitting the check — and say out loud, at least to yourself, 'I did that on purpose.'
4.core:
There's a fairness running through how you handle what sits between you and other people. You notice when someone's shorted, you adjust without announcing it, you hand back what came to you. That's reciprocal, and it isn't automatic — it's you doing it. You'd call it practical. Just being reasonable. The accounting gets done and gets filed under nothing special.

That's the part that belongs to you and hasn't been claimed. The steady back-and-forth isn't a background condition of life; it's something you're running. No need to announce it to the people around you. The work is to stop letting it count as background.
4.sheetLine: You've been keeping things even and calling it 'nothing much.'
